title: What do living things need?
intro: Identify the needs of plants and animals. Explain how the place they live helps meet those needs.
exampleTitle: Water is one need, not every need
example: A potted plant near a window has access to light and air. Its roots take up water. A plant needs suitable growing conditions; watering alone does not replace light. Animals need suitable food, water and air, and places that protect them.
evidence:
Living thingNeedWhat the place provides
Potted plantLightA suitable bright position
Garden birdWaterA clean water source
Garden birdShelterSuitable protected places
steps: Name the need
Start with what the living thing needs, rather than an object you would like to give it.

AnimalPlant
Air, water, suitable food and shelterAir, water, light and suitable growing conditions
Does a toy meet a rabbit’s need for water?
No. A toy may provide activity, but the rabbit still needs suitable drinking water.
Match a place to a need
Look for a feature that supplies a need. A birdbath may supply water; leafy cover may provide shelter.

Need → feature

Water → water source. Shelter → a suitable protected place.
Does shelter also provide every animal with food?
No. Check each need separately and consider the particular animal.
Compare and care
Living things share needs, but the amount of water and suitable food or shelter can differ. Observe and ask an adult how to care for them.

Two plants, different care

A cactus and a fern both need water. They may need different amounts and conditions.
Must every animal eat seeds?
No. Different animals need different foods. Never feed a wild animal just to test an idea.
mistakes: “Soil is a plant’s food.”
Plants make their own food using light. Roots take up water and nutrients; soil can also support the plant.
“Water is all it needs.”
Check all the needs. Do not remove a plant’s or animal’s necessities to test this.
activity: 2 minutes: choose a familiar plant or animal with an adult. 5 minutes: draw its home and label three features that help meet its needs. 3 minutes: explain each need → feature link.
adjust: Support: use picture choices. Extend: compare two living things and explain one difference in their needs.
safety: Observe without disturbing wildlife. Follow an adult’s care guidance.
tricky: A pet has a roof over its enclosure. Have all its needs been met?
No. Shelter alone does not supply air, water and suitable food.
Two plants need different amounts of water. Does only one need water?
No. Both need water; their suitable conditions differ.
Can a rock provide shelter for a small animal?
It can provide a protected space for some animals. Observe without lifting or moving its shelter.
faq: Do plants eat soil?
No. Plants make their own food using light. Soil may supply water, nutrients and support.
What is a habitat?
The place a living thing lives, with features that can meet its needs.

title: What changed outside?
intro: Describe changes during a day and across seasons. Connect the changes to what people, plants and animals do.
example: In this example, the morning is cloudy. Rain falls after lunch. We choose a raincoat for going outside. This is a change during one day; it does not identify the whole season.
evidence:
WhenObservationEveryday response
MorningCloudy skyCheck the forecast before an outing
After lunchRain fallingWear suitable wet-weather clothing
steps: Record a daily change
Notice the sky, temperature or light at different times. A day's weather can change.

MorningAfter lunch
CloudyRainy
Are these records from two different seasons?
No. They describe different times on the same day.
Look across many days
Seasonal patterns involve changes over longer periods, such as typical weather, flowering or animal activity. One unusual day is not a whole seasonal pattern.

Local evidence matters

Compare dated observations over time. Different Australian places have different seasonal patterns.
Does a cold day prove it is winter?
No. Cold days can occur outside winter. Use the date, place and observations over time.
Connect changes to life
People adjust clothing and activities. Plants and animals may also change as local conditions change.

Observed conditionPossible response
RainyWear a raincoat
Hot and sunnySeek shade and follow sun protection advice
Must every Australian place have snow in winter?
No. Winter conditions vary across Australia. Describe local evidence.
mistakes: “Weather and season mean the same thing.”
Weather describes conditions at a time; seasonal patterns are seen across a longer period.
“All seasonal calendars are the same.”
First Nations seasonal knowledge is specific to particular Countries, Peoples and local indicators. Use an appropriate community-approved source.
activity: 2 minutes: observe safely from a window. 5 minutes: draw the sky and choose clothing suited to today's conditions. 3 minutes: explain the connection. Add another dated record later to compare.
adjust: Support: choose from weather pictures. Extend: compare today's record with an earlier dated record; say what more is needed to study a season.
safety: Never look directly at the Sun. Observe storms indoors.
tricky: It rains in summer. Has the season become winter?
No. A rainy day can occur in summer.
A tree has fewer leaves today. Can we say why from that alone?
No. Compare earlier records and local information. Different plants behave differently.
Can two places have different weather on the same day?
Yes. Record the place as well as the time.
faq: What counts as a daily change?
A change during one day, such as light, temperature or rainfall.
Can we use local First Nations seasonal knowledge?
Yes, with locally appropriate, community-approved sources and respect for cultural authority.

title: Push, pull and predict
intro: Describe the strength and direction of pushes and pulls. Predict changes to an object's motion or shape.
example: Push a toy car gently to the right, then try a stronger push with the same car, start point and surface. Predict that it may travel farther after the stronger push. Observe what actually happens. A push on soft dough may change its shape instead.
evidence:
ActionDirection or strengthPossible effect
Push a carTo the rightStarts moving right
Stronger push, otherwise similar trialGreater strengthMay travel farther
Press soft doughInwardsChanges shape
steps: Name the force and direction
A force is a push or pull. Describe which way it acts. Force direction and movement direction are not always the same.

Examples

Push a toy car away from your hand. Pull a toy wagon towards you using its handle.
A ball rolls right. A hand pushes against it to the left. Could it slow down?
Yes. A push opposite to its movement can slow or stop it.
Compare strengths carefully
Change the strength of the push while keeping the car, surface and starting place the same. Predict before trying.

TrialCar and surfacePush
ASame car and boardGentle
BSame car and boardStronger
Can we compare push strength if one trial uses a heavy car on a rug and the other a light car on a board?
The comparison is unclear because the car and surface changed too.
Watch motion and shape
A force may start, stop, speed up, slow down or turn an object. It may also bend, stretch or squash a suitable material.

ObjectActionObservation
Soft doughPress gentlyShape changes
Moving carOpposing pushMay slow or stop
Does every force make an object move to a new place?
No. An object may stay in place or change shape.
mistakes: “A stronger push always moves every object farther.”
Compare the same object and conditions. Other conditions and obstacles can affect the result.
“Only pulling can change shape.”
A push can squash dough; a pull can stretch suitable material.
activity: 2 minutes: an adult checks a floor-level space and a sturdy toy car. 5 minutes: compare gentle and stronger pushes from the same start; then gently press soft dough. 3 minutes: describe direction, strength and the observed effects.
adjust: Support: point and say push or pull. Extend: explain which conditions must stay the same to compare push strength.
safety: Use gentle forces away from people, edges and breakable objects. Use dough only if suitable for the child; do not eat it.
tricky: Can a force stop a moving object?
Yes. A force acting against motion can slow or stop it.
A pushed box does not move. Was there necessarily no push?
No. A push may act even when no movement is visible.
Can the same material change shape in more than one way?
Yes. Suitable dough can be squashed by pushing or stretched by pulling.
faq: Is a force just movement?
No. A force is a push or pull that can affect motion or shape.
Do we need force calculations?
No. Describe and compare familiar pushes and pulls using everyday language.

title: Use science in everyday life
intro: Describe how people use science each day. Use observed patterns to make useful predictions.
example: A gardener has noticed that this pot's soil often dries more quickly on warm days. On another warm day, the gardener predicts it may be dry. They check the plant's needs and soil before deciding whether to water.
evidence:
EvidencePredictionUseful action
This pot often dries on warm daysIt may be dry todayCheck the plant and soil with an adult
steps: Find an everyday use
Science helps people care for plants and animals, plan for weather and design useful tools.

PersonUses observations to…
GardenerCheck plant care
Wildlife carerProvide suitable shelter
FamilyPlan clothing for the weather
Is science only used in a laboratory?
No. People use observations and scientific knowledge in many daily activities.
Use a pattern to predict
A prediction uses relevant experience to say what may happen. It is not a guarantee.

Pattern → prediction

The path was slippery after earlier rain. After more rain, it may be slippery again.
Is “It may be wet because rain is forecast” a prediction?
Yes. It predicts a possibility and gives a relevant reason.
Check before deciding
Observe what happens and adjust the action. People also learn from local experts and knowledge holders.

Knowledge and place

Learn about local living things from gardeners or carers. First Nations knowledge belongs to particular Peoples and Countries; use authorised local sources.
Should a gardener water every plant just because today is warm?
No. Check the particular plant, soil and care guidance first.
mistakes: “A prediction must come true.”
A prediction can differ from what happens. Keep the evidence and check again.
“One care rule suits every habitat.”
Different plants, animals and places have different needs.
activity: 2 minutes: choose a familiar task such as checking a plant or planning clothing. 5 minutes: draw the evidence, prediction and decision. 3 minutes: explain how science helped.
adjust: Support: complete “I noticed… so I might…”. Extend: explain what observation could make you change your decision.
safety: An adult makes care and weather-safety decisions.
tricky: An outing forecast changes. Must the family keep its first plan?
No. Use new information to adjust the plan.
Can a wildlife carer use science without wearing a lab coat?
Yes. Observing animals' needs and designing suitable support use science.
Is “because I like yellow” evidence that a raincoat is needed?
No. Use weather information or observations.
faq: What is a scientific prediction?
A statement about what may happen, supported by relevant observations or experience.
Can tools use science?
Yes. Designers use knowledge of materials and pushes and pulls to make tools useful.

title: Notice, wonder, predict
intro: Ask questions about simple patterns you observe. Make a prediction using relevant experience.
exampleTitle: Will the car go farther on the board again?
example: In earlier similar trials, a toy car travelled farther on a board than on a rug. We ask whether that pattern will happen again. We predict it may travel farther on the board, using the earlier records as our reason.
evidence:
Earlier trialBoardRug
16 equal block lengths3 equal block lengths
25 equal block lengths3 equal block lengths
steps: Say what you noticed
An observation reports what happened. It is different from a guess about the next trial.

Observation

In trial 1, the car travelled 6 block lengths on the board.
Which reports an observation: “It travelled 6 blocks” or “It may travel 6 blocks next time”?
“It travelled 6 blocks” reports what happened.
Ask about the pattern
Choose a question that observation or a safe investigation could help answer.

QuestionCan this investigate rolling distance?
Does the car go farther on the board or rug?Yes
Which surface do I like best?No: that asks a preference
What question could you ask after noticing a plant lean towards a window?
For example: “Does the plant keep leaning towards the window as it grows?” Observe without harming it.
Predict and give a reason
Predict before the next observation. Use relevant earlier evidence and words such as may or might.

Sentence frame

I predict __ because I noticed __.
Must you change your prediction if the next result is different?
Keep the original prediction and record the actual result. You can revise a later prediction using the new evidence.
mistakes: “Any guess is a reasoned prediction.”
Give relevant experience or a pattern as your reason.
“One result proves it always happens.”
Look for more observations and consider the conditions.
activityTitle: Ask a question from a record
activity: 2 minutes: read the supplied car records. 5 minutes: say one observation, ask one question and write or dictate a prediction with a reason. 3 minutes: explain which evidence supports it.
adjust: Support: use sentence starters. Extend: name one condition that would need to stay similar in another trial.
safety: If testing, use an adult-checked floor-level setup and sturdy toys.
tricky: Is “The car is blue” a reason it will travel farther?
No. Colour alone is not relevant distance evidence in this comparison.
Can a question be useful even if we do not know its answer yet?
Yes. The question guides what to observe or investigate.
A result disagrees with your prediction. Did you fail to learn anything?
No. Record it accurately and ask a connected question.
faq: What is the difference between a question and a prediction?
A question asks what we want to find out. A prediction says what we think may happen.
Do predictions need reasons?
Use relevant experiences or observed patterns to support them.

title: Plan a safe investigation
intro: Suggest and follow safe steps that help investigate a question and test a prediction.
exampleTitle: A safe plan for the toy-car question
example: Question: does the car travel farther on the board or rug? With an adult, choose a clear floor-level space. Use the same car and start mark. Try a similar gentle push on each surface, observe and record, then pack away.
evidence:
OrderProcedureWhy
1Adult checks space and equipmentAvoid hazards
2Try the agreed comparisonTest the question
3Record, then pack awayKeep evidence and clear the space
steps: Connect steps to the question
Choose actions that can provide the observation you need. Predict before testing.

We need to observe…

How far this car travels on each surface, not which colour children prefer.
Would measuring the car's colour test which surface lets it travel farther?
No. The plan needs observations of distance travelled.
Check safety first
An adult checks equipment and space. Stop and tell an adult if anything breaks or spills.

HazardSafer procedure
Objects near an edgeWork at floor level
People in the pathClear the test space
Broken toyStop and tell an adult
Should you continue with a broken toy because the test is nearly finished?
No. Stop and tell an adult.
Follow, record and reflect
Follow agreed steps in order. Keep the comparison useful, record results and explain a possible improvement.

Keep similar

Same car, starting place and push approach. Change the surface being compared.
Why use the same car in both trials?
It helps us compare the surfaces without also changing the car.
mistakes: “Safe steps can come after the test.”
Check the plan and hazards before starting.
“Any safe activity answers the question.”
The steps must also produce relevant evidence.
activity: 2 minutes: an adult reads the question with you. 5 minutes: draw a safe setup and arrange prepare → try → record cards. 3 minutes: explain one safety choice and one step that answers the question.
adjust: Support: order picture cards. Extend: identify a change that would make the comparison less useful.
safety: Do not investigate heat, sharp tools, electricity or unknown substances in this activity.
tricky: The toy is safe, but a person is sitting in its path. Is the setup ready?
No. The space needs to be clear too.
Can a drawing help someone follow a procedure?
Yes, if it shows the equipment and steps clearly.
A spill occurs during the test. Should you record first?
Stop and tell an adult. Make the area safe before continuing.
faq: What is a procedure?
A clear set of steps to follow.
Can children suggest changes?
Yes. Discuss them with an adult and check safety before trying them.

title: Observe, measure and record
intro: Record what you observe. Use informal measurements and appropriate tools so another person can understand your record.
example: A strip exactly spans five identical blocks laid end to end with no gaps or overlaps. Record “5 block lengths”, not just “5”. A labelled drawing or photograph can preserve details; it still needs the object and unit explained.
evidence:
ObjectInformal measurementHow measured
Strip A5 block lengthsEqual blocks, end to end
Strip B3 block lengthsThe same size blocks
steps: Observe rather than invent
Use appropriate senses and safe tools to notice features. Separate what you see from a possible explanation.

Observation

I can see two holes in this leaf. That does not by itself show what made them.
Does a leaf with holes prove a caterpillar made them?
No. Record the holes; the cause needs more evidence.
Measure consistently
Use equal informal units, align the start, and leave no gaps or overlaps. Include the unit name.

Clear recordUnclear record
Length: 5 block lengthsLength: 5
Could five large blocks and five small blocks represent different lengths?
Yes. Use the same-size units when comparing measurements.
Choose a useful record
A labelled drawing, dated photograph, tally or table can show observations. Choose a tool that preserves the detail you need.

Record label

Object: strip A. Date: __. Length: 5 block lengths. Unit: our identical wooden blocks.
Is an unlabelled photograph enough to explain when and what you measured?
Not always. Add the object, date and measurement information.
mistakes: “Bigger units give a bigger count.”
A longer unit may fit fewer times into the same length.
“A photograph explains everything.”
Add labels and context; do not claim details the image does not show.
activity: 2 minutes: choose a strip and identical large blocks with an adult. 5 minutes: measure with no gaps, draw the result and name the unit. 3 minutes: ask a partner to explain your record.
adjust: Support: use a strip that exactly spans whole blocks. Extend: explain why a different-sized unit could change the count.
safety: Use safe objects and an adult-approved digital device. Photograph objects rather than people's private details.
tricky: Two children record 5 units but use different unit sizes. Must the lengths match?
No. The unit sizes matter.
You forget the measurement. Should you write a likely number?
No. Measure again if possible and record the observation.
A strip ends between two blocks. Should you claim it is exactly 5 blocks?
No. Describe it as between the nearby whole-block measurements or use a more suitable unit with guidance.
faq: What is an informal unit?
An everyday unit such as an identical block, rather than a standard unit such as a centimetre.
Must every record be written?
No. Labelled drawings, photographs and dictated observations can also communicate evidence.

title: Sort the evidence. Show the pattern.
intro: Sort and order observations. Use provided tables and visual or physical models to show patterns accurately.
exampleTitle: More flowers, then the same number
example: A class records open flowers on the same plant at the same time on three days. The supplied counts are 2, 4 and 4. Keep the dates in order: the count increases, then stays the same.
steps: Choose a sorting rule
Group records by a named feature. Keep the rule consistent and explain uncertain cases.

RecordGroup: rain observed?
Rain fallingYes
Clear sky, no rain seenNo
If you sort leaves by shape, should colour decide the group?
No. Use the chosen shape rule. You can sort by colour in a separate sort.
Order and label the data
Use date order for changes over time. Match each value to its correct label.

Correct date orderCounts
Day 1 → Day 2 → Day 32 → 4 → 4
Should you reorder the days to make the numbers go 2, 4, 4, 6?
No. Preserve the real dates and counts. Do not invent a fourth record.
Build a faithful model
In a one-to-one display, one counter represents one observation. Use the same meaning throughout.

DayOne counter = one flower
1● ●
2● ● ● ●
3● ● ● ●
What happened between days 2 and 3?
The count stayed the same at 4. It did not increase.
mistakes: “A pattern must keep increasing.”
The count may decrease or stay the same. Report what the records show.
“We may add counters to make the picture look full.”
Every counter must match the chosen key and recorded data.
activity: 2 minutes: read the 2, 4, 4 flower records. 5 minutes: make three labelled rows with large counters or drawn circles. 3 minutes: describe the change and check each row against the table.
adjust: Support: use one-to-one drawn circles. Extend: represent the same records another way and check that the message stays the same.
safety: Choose counters suitable for the child's age; drawings work just as well.
tricky: Two rows have four counters each. Did the number increase?
No. It stayed the same.
Can one counter mean one flower in one row and two flowers in another?
Not in this one-to-one display. Keep the key consistent.
Does a bigger drawing of a flower mean more flowers?
No. Count or read the key; picture size alone does not show number.
faq: What is data?
Recorded observations or information.
Must every pattern repeat?
No. A pattern can show change or sameness across ordered records.

title: Did the result match?
intro: Compare results with predictions and others' observations. With guidance, consider fairness and ask a further question.
example: Before a car trial, Mia predicts 3 block lengths. Afterwards, she measures 5 block lengths. She keeps both records: the observation is farther than predicted. Another group records 4 block lengths; they compare their units and setup before explaining the difference.
evidence:
RecordDistance
Prediction, before trial3 block lengths
Observation, after trial5 block lengths
Another group4 block lengths
steps: Compare prediction and observation
A prediction says what may happen. An observation records what did happen. Keep both.

BeforeAfter
I predict 3 block lengthsWe observed 5 block lengths
Should Mia change her prediction to 5 after measuring?
No. Keep the prediction as 3 and the observation as 5.
Compare other records
Describe similarities and differences. Ask about the car, surface, push and units before assuming anyone is wrong.

Our result / their result

We recorded 5 block lengths. They recorded 4. Did we use the same-sized blocks and similar conditions?
Do different records prove someone was careless?
No. Conditions or measurement methods may differ. Investigate with guidance.
Check fairness and ask next
A useful comparison changes what is being investigated while keeping other important conditions similar.

Comparing surfacesWhat should stay similar?
Board versus rugSame car, starting point, push approach and measurement units
What further question follows these results?
For example: “Will the same car travel similar distances if we repeat the trial using the same setup?”
mistakes: “A wrong prediction ruins the investigation.”
An honest result can teach us something even when it differs from the prediction.
“A fair test means everyone gets a turn.”
Taking turns is fair behaviour. A fair comparison also needs suitable test conditions.
activity: 2 minutes: read the prediction and observation table. 5 minutes: mark match or differ and explain the difference. 3 minutes: ask about another group's setup and suggest one connected question.
adjust: Support: use before/after cards. Extend: identify two changes that could make a surface comparison unclear.
safety: Use supplied records or an adult-checked safe setup.
tricky: The result is different from the prediction. Which should be erased?
Neither. Keep both so you can compare them.
One group uses a ramp and another a flat start. Can surface alone explain the different distances?
No. The starting setup changed too.
Can a repeated investigation give a slightly different result?
Yes. Compare methods and evidence before making a claim.
faq: What does compare mean?
Describe what is the same and what is different.
What makes a further question useful?
It connects to the evidence and can guide another observation or safe investigation.

title: Make your science message clear
intro: Write and create texts that communicate observations, findings and ideas. Use clear everyday and scientific vocabulary.
exampleTitle: Tell the reader what the car test showed
example: A class's supplied records show 6 block lengths on a board and 3 on a rug. A useful report names the object, surfaces and unit: “In our trial, the toy car travelled farther on the board than on the rug.” It does not claim the same result will happen in every possible trial.
evidence:
SurfaceObserved distance
Board6 block lengths
Rug3 block lengths
steps: Choose the evidence
Tell what you observed. Keep guesses about a cause separate from findings.

Evidence-based sentence

In our trial, the car travelled 6 block lengths on the board.
Is “The car was happy on the board” a scientific observation?
No. Report observable movement or measurements rather than an imagined feeling.
Use labels and useful words
A drawing, table or short text should name the object and important features. Use words such as push, surface and distance when they help.

UnclearClearer
It went over thereThe toy car moved to the right
It went 6It travelled 6 block lengths
Which label would improve a drawing of this test?
For example: toy car, board, rug, start mark or the measurement unit, placed beside the correct feature.
Organise and check the message
Choose a short report, labelled drawing or table for your audience. Re-read it with the records. Ask a partner what they understood.

Mini-report

We tested a toy car on two surfaces. In our trial it travelled 6 block lengths on the board and 3 on the rug. It travelled farther on the board.
Can we conclude that every car always travels twice as far on every board?
No. These records describe this trial and setup; they do not establish a universal rule.
mistakes: “More science words always make a report better.”
Choose accurate words your audience can understand.
“A neat picture can replace the evidence.”
Include labels and observations that match the actual record.
activity: 2 minutes: read the car results. 5 minutes: create a labelled drawing, table or two-sentence report. 3 minutes: ask a partner to explain the finding and improve one unclear label.
adjust: Support: dictate a sentence and add picture labels. Extend: include a further question and clearly separate it from the finding.
safety: Use supplied records. Share images or recordings only with an adult's guidance.
tricky: Can a report be clear even if it uses everyday words?
Yes. Accurate everyday words can communicate well; add scientific vocabulary where useful.
The table says 3 blocks. Should the report say 4 because the picture looks longer?
No. Check the record and report its evidence accurately.
Can a finding and a new question appear in the same report?
Yes. Label them clearly so the reader knows which is evidence and which asks what to investigate next.
faq: What is a finding?
What the observations or results show in the investigation.
Can we learn other ways of sharing observations?
Yes. Use culturally appropriate authorised examples when learning about particular First Nations Peoples' ways of communicating knowledge.
